title: Multiple nivolumab-induced CNS demyelination with spontaneous resolution in an asymptomatic metastatic melanoma patient
case_prompt:
A 44-year-old man with stage IIIB cutaneous nodular melanoma of the right forearm underwent wide local excision, axillary lymph node dissection, and adjuvant ipilimumab (discontinued after one dose due to corticosteroid-resistant colitis). He subsequently had a wedge resection of a PD-L1–positive pulmonary metastasis and received stereotactic radiosurgery to five small brain metastases followed by nivolumab monotherapy (3 mg/kg every 2 weeks).  
Two weeks after the first nivolumab infusion, he developed asthenia, headache, and right upper-limb apraxia; new cerebral lesions were treated with dexamethasone. He later had a generalized seizure, was started on levetiracetam, and underwent further stereotactic radiosurgery for additional metastases. Nivolumab was resumed in February 2018.  
A follow-up brain MRI in April 2018 showed shrinkage or disappearance of prior lesions. In June 2018, after 11 cycles of nivolumab, a routine brain MRI revealed multiple new, well-defined, ovoid lesions in the juxtacortical and periventricular white matter. These lesions were T2-hyperintense, demonstrated incomplete (open) ring enhancement after contrast, showed hypovascularization on perfusion imaging, and had no diffusion restriction.  
The patient remained completely asymptomatic; neurologic examination and EEG were unchanged, and there were no systemic signs of infection or melanoma progression.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Brain metastases were considered but excluded because “previously treated brain metastases were T2-hypointense with central necrosis and large perilesional oedema, had complete ring enhancement on post-contrast T1-weighted imaging and hypervascularization on perfusion weighted imaging.”  
2. Leptomeningeal carcinomatosis was considered as progressive oncologic disease but ruled out as “all other differential diagnoses have been ruled out, including brain metastasis and leptomeningeal carcinomatosis for progressive oncologic disease.”  
3. Multiple sclerosis was considered among CNS demyelinating diseases but excluded since “all other differential diagnoses have been ruled out … but also other demyelinating diseases of the CNS like multiple sclerosis.”  
4. Vascular causes were excluded because “MRI revealed no evidence of ischemic or haemorrhagic events.”  
5. Infection was excluded on the basis that “there were no findings indicating an infection.”  
6. Ipilimumab-induced demyelination was considered unlikely as “the long interval of 12 months between the unique dose of ipilimumab and the occurrence of CNS demyelination argues against a role of this antibody.”  
7. Immune-related toxicity from nivolumab was favored because “the onset and improvement of radiological lesions correlates with the administration and discontinuation of nivolumab, respectively, … indicates that CNS toxicity is most likely nivolumab-related.”
